title: How to show marketing’s impact on pipeline with buying-committee evidence
summary: Attribution fights over credit. Learn how to show which people on the buying committee marketing reached on each deal, and what wins have that losses don’t.
body_markdown:
“So what did marketing do on this one?”


Your biggest deal of the quarter just closed, and your CEO wants an answer. You pull up the attribution report. Fourteen campaigns touched the deal. A webinar gets 22% of the credit. The other 13 split the rest.


Your Sales team says the AE found the deal. You say the ads warmed it up. Neither of you can prove it.


If you’ve sat through some version of that meeting, plenty of other marketers feel your pain. In our[Reality of ABM survey (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/guides-and-reports/reality-of-abm-report) of 239 B2B marketers, only 15.9% said they can immediately show evidence everyone agrees on when leadership or sales questions marketing’s contribution to pipeline.


Most of the rest are doing cleanup. For 30.5%, the number holds up, but only after someone investigates. For 25.9%, marketing and sales look at the same evidence and read it differently. And 22.2% rebuild the story by hand.


## Attribution answers the wrong question


Attribution asks which touch gets credit. That fight rarely ends, because[every model rests on assumptions (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/account-based-marketing-attribution) about what caused the deal, and Sales and Marketing start from different ones.


As one respondent put it: “everyone wants attribution but it is not real in the way they want it.”


Credit isn’t the only thing marketers are after, either. When we asked what they’d most want to be true if their ABM program worked exactly the way they wanted, 23.8% picked a clear picture of what sales and marketing each did to win a deal. Nearly the same share (23.4%) picked proving marketing’s revenue.


That picture starts with a simpler question you can answer: did marketing reach the people who bought?


Did the VP who signed see your ads before the first meeting? Did the RevOps lead who blocked the last deal read your integration page this time? Did the engagement come from one champion, or from the whole committee?


## See every deal person by person


Vector’s[Journeys (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/platform/journeys) view puts the account and each buyer in it on one timeline: their signals, the marketing touches that reached them, and sales activity. Click any event to see what happened, who it involved, when, and which campaign it came from. When a deal opens or closes,[Stories (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/platform/stories) writes it up for you, with the buyers involved, the key marketing moments, and the ads that touched it.


So in the deal review, you can walk through it buyer by buyer: the economic buyer saw your ads for six weeks before the first meeting, the ops lead read the integration docs twice during evaluation, and the champion’s boss engaged for the first time the week before close.

None of those moments is a click or a form fill, so a report[built on clicks and form fills (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/the-attribution-black-hole-how-to-prove-b2b-marketing-impact-without-form-fills) could miss most of that story. Getting leadership to count them is its own fight. When we asked what frustrates them most about ABM, one respondent wrote:


“Shifting leadership’s definition of success beyond ‘did this channel generate a lead?’ to include channel influence. As in, the ads that don’t get clicked but shape intent, and the touchpoints that don’t appear in a CRM report but move deals forward.”


## Be clear about what it proves


What you’re showing is[evidence of reach (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/abm-measurement) . It shows marketing was in front of the right people at the right time. It doesn’t show they bought *because* of it.


Say that in the meeting. A list of the people you reached is easier for a CFO to check than a percentage from a model.


Then agree on what counts before you report[influenced pipeline (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/marketing-influenced-vs-sourced-pipeline) . Sit down with Sales and RevOps once and settle which engagement types count, what time window applies, and whether it has to happen before the opp is created. Write the definition down and use it every quarter.


The same journey that shows why an account changed stage also shows who marketing reached on the deal. In our survey, teams that can almost always[explain why an account’s stage changed (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/specter-abm-account-scoring) were nearly four times as likely to immediately show pipeline evidence everyone agrees on (29.5% vs. 7.5% of teams that rarely can).


## Compare what you won to what you lost


One deal won’t tell you much on its own. Put your recent closed-won deals next to your closed-lost ones and compare the committees:


-


Did you reach more roles on the deals you won?


-


Is there a role, like Ops or Finance, that shows up engaged in wins and missing in losses?


-


Did engagement start earlier on the wins?

If the budget owner is dark on most of the deals you lose, start there. That’s the role your next campaign needs to reach.


## Run it this week


You’ll get more out of this with someone who knows the deals. Ask your AE or a RevOps partner to sit in on the first pass. They’ll know which losses came down to timing or budget, so you can set those aside and focus on the deals where the committee might have made the difference.


1. 1


**Pull five closed-won and five closed-lost deals** from the last two quarters.


2. 2


**Map the committee on each.** Note who marketing reached and when.


3. 3


**Find one difference** between the wins and the losses.


4. 4


**Change one thing.** Build an audience or message aimed at that gap, using the same approach as our[buying committee play (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/how-to-reach-your-b2b-buying-committee-with-contact-level-ads) , now aimed with evidence.


5. 5


**Share it.** Bring one deal story to your next pipeline review.


If the gaps you find start earlier in the deal, we’ve also covered[finding the people inside your accounts (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/how-to-find-in-market-buyers-not-just-in-market-accounts) and[getting buyers to Sales while they’re still evaluating (opens in a new tab)](https://www.vector.co/blog/how-to-turn-anonymous-buyer-activity-into-qualified-pipeline) .


The next time your CEO asks what marketing did on a deal, bring the people you reached and what you’re changing to reach the ones you missed.
